A minimal reproducible example (MRE) is essential for fixing bugs. Without an example that can be used to reproduce the problem, a maintainer cannot debug it or test if it is fixed. ## How to write a reproducible example. When writing a reproducible example, the goal is to provide all the context necessary for someone else to reproduce your example. Below, we'll cover several specific strategies for creating and sharing reproducible examples. ## Strategies for reproducible examples. Writing a Docker image is often the best way to share a reproducible example because it is entirely self-contained. Using a Docker image is only feasible if the issue is reproducible on Linux. When using macOS, it's prudent to ensure your image is not reproducible on Linux but some bugs *are* specific to the operating system. When writing a Docker MRE with uv, it's best to start with one of uv's Docker images. When sharing a reproduction, you can explicitly set the platform to ensure a reproducer gets the expected behavior. Docker images are best for reproducing issues that can be constructed with commands, e.g.:. If you need to write many files, it's better to create and publish a Git repository. When sharing a Docker reproduction, it's helpful to include the build logs. When reporting platform-specific bugs that cannot be reproduced in a container, it's best practice to include a script showing the commands that can be used to reproduce the bug, e.g.:. If your reproduction requires many files, use a Git repository to share them. For example, if you wrote the script on Windows, and it uses a Python version that you installed with `choco` and runs on PowerShell 6.2, please include that in the report. When sharing a Git repository reproduction, include a script that reproduces the problem or, even better, a Dockerfile. When using a Git repository for a reproduction, please remember to *minimize* the contents by excluding files or settings that are not required to reproduce your problem.

An introduction to Docker for reproducible research, with examples from the R environment. As computational work becomes more and more integral to many aspects of scientific research, computational reproducibility has become an issue of increasing importance to computer systems researchers and domain scientists alike. Though computational reproducibility seems more straight forward than replicating physical experiments, the complex and rapidly changing nature of computer environments makes being able to reproduce and extend such work a serious challenge. I then examine how the popular emerging technology Docker combines several areas from systems research - such as operating system virtualization, cross-platform portability, modular re-usable elements, versioning, and a `DevOps' philosophy, to address these challenges. Container technologies emerged as a leading approach to address reproducibility challenges by providing isolated execution environments. This was achieved using the Docker platform (113), and we used a minimal Debian-based Docker image from the Rocker Project ( images/) to ensure a reproducible and portable R environment for our analysis. Furthermore, to ensure computational reproducibility, we resorted to containerize our working environment, code, and data using the Docker ecosystem 99 . A custom, running instance of our container (i.e., Docker Image) is made available from the Docker Hub container registry. Based on these experiences, we argue: it is sometimes reasonable to use an older kernel version, experimental results need careful analysis to explain why a performance effect occurs, and publishing papers validating prior research is essential. results.content: MGFX - A cross-platform 2D (CPU & GPU) and 3D (GPU) starter kit. 39 stars 7 forks Branches Tags Activity. # MGFX - Cross-platform 2D (CPU & GPU) and 3D (GPU) rendering starter kit. An example of how to do cross-platform 2D (CPU & GPU) and 3D (GPU) rendering. The project is also a useful guide for how to build an open source project with continuous integration, cmake, documentation and unit tests. There is a sample here of drawing a 3D Scene, or you can use it to draw to an RGBA memory buffer using the CPU, and transfer it to the screen. In 3D Mode, a simple mesh loader is provided, which loads a custom mesh format. A tool - MGeo is also supplied to load many mesh formats and convert them to the binary format used - based on Google Flatbuffers. The mgfx\_core library has the common code for setting up a device and managing 2D & 3D setup, such as adding cameras and windows. The mcommon folder contains useful C++ code for things like manipulating files. ## MGeo. This simple convertor uses Assimp to load a 3D Mesh, then outputs an optimized 3D mesh for rendering. Once the mesh is processed, it is output using a flatbuffer file format schema. I used this project as a learning experience for setting up Open Source continuous integration builds. The `config_lean.bat` file make a more minimal configuration that doesn't build MGeo or the associated libraries (not required for the demo). Type `CTest --verbose` in the build folder to run unit tests. Microsoft's solution uses a custom binary file format, but my approach uses a more flexible flatbuffer approach. SDL2 is used to get a window on the screen in a cross platform way, and for OpenGL to generate a Context. There are many useful things in the STB library; I am using it here to load PNG texture files. The MGeo project builds it on demand, since it is a big library.
